youtube_title: X-Men Toys Were Ruled 'Not Human' — to Cut Import Duty 🦝⚖️
caption: In Toy Biz v. United States (2003), the trade court held X-Men figures weren't 'dolls representing only human beings' because of non-human features — putting them in a lower-duty toy category under the tariff schedule of the time.
script: The company selling X-Men toys argued its action figures were not human. And it won. This was a U.S. trade court decision from twenty oh-three. Under the tariff schedule at the time, dolls, meaning figures representing only human beings, carried a twelve percent duty. Toys representing animals or non-human creatures, like robots and monsters, carried six point eight percent. Customs said the X-Men figures were dolls. The importer, Toy Biz, said: look closer. These are mutants. Wolverine has claws. Other figures had fangs or tentacles. The court agreed. It said even one non-human feature could keep a figure out of the doll category. And it pointed out that these characters are known for being more than, or different from, human. So the X-Men went into the lower-duty toy category. Not every figure won, by the way. A different toy in the same case was ruled a doll. Here's the limit. This was about physical toys and the tariff categories back then. By twenty oh-two, the schedule had already made all of these toy categories duty-free going forward. And it says nothing about anyone's actual humanity. [loop] So the next time someone calls your action figure a doll, remember
